## Summary Scores

-   **Sensitivity:** Low
-   **Exposure:** High
-   **Vulnerability:** Low

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the directory and the correct file extension pattern
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "\\.pdf$", "\\.png$")
dir_path <- here::here("figures/Longfin squid")

# Search for any file containing the string AND the correct extension
found_files <- list.files(
  path = dir_path, 
  pattern = paste0("combined_table_allvars.*", ext), 
  full.names = TRUE
)

has_figure <- length(found_files) > 0

if (has_figure) {
  # Get metadata for all matching files
  file_details <- file.info(found_files)
  
  # Find the row with the maximum (newest) modification time
  newest_index <- which.max(file_details$mtime)
  
  # Assign the newest file's path to img_path
  img_path <- found_files[newest_index]
} else {
  img_path <- NULL
}
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| lightbox: true
#| out-width: "100%"
#| label: fig-sum-tab-longfin

Exposure and Vulnerability scores are averaged spatially across the species distribution and within stocks if applicable (see @fig-vuln-longfin and @fig-exp-longfin). Life History Data Quality (LH DQ) and Standard Deviations (SD) are reported for senstivity and exposure/vulnerability scores, respectively."
#| fig-pos: "H"

knitr::include_graphics(img_path)
```

## Score Descriptions:

### Sensitivity:

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Define the directory and the correct file extension pattern
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), "\\.pdf$", "\\.png$")
dir_path <- here::here("figures/Longfin squid")

# Search for any file containing the string AND the correct extension
found_files <- list.files(
  path = dir_path, 
  pattern = paste0("sensitivity.*", ext), 
  full.names = TRUE
)

has_figure <- length(found_files) > 0

if (has_figure) {
  # Get metadata for all matching files
  file_details <- file.info(found_files)
  
  # Find the row with the maximum (newest) modification time
  newest_index <- which.max(file_details$mtime)
  
  # Assign the newest file's path to img_path
  img_path <- found_files[newest_index]
} else {
  img_path <- NULL
}

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result 
has_figure <- file.exists(img_path)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Longfin squid Sensitivity on the Northeast Shelf"
#| label: fig-sens-longfin
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"

knitr::include_graphics(img_path)
```

Long-finned squid received a **Low** sensitivity score. Certainty was 98% according to bootstrap results. No attributes scored greater than 2.5. Complexity in Reproductive Strategy received the highest score (2.4) (@fig-sum-tab-longfin). Eggs are cemented to bottom substrate, which can include algae and boulders that may be impacted by dredging activities in nearshore spawning grounds [@jacobson2005essential] [@guyant2022northeast].

Long-finned squid also received a Low sensitivity score in the previous Climate Vulnerability Assessment for the Northeast Shelf. Similar to our results, this previous score was driven by Early Life History Requirements due to the benthic egg masses of this species [@hare2016vulnerability].

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure

#| fig-pos: "H"
knitr::include_graphics(img_path)
```

Mean Exposure for Longfin squid was **High** (3.02 +/- 0.54) (@fig-sum-tab-longfin). Exposure was high throughout the continental shelf. Scores were Very High over Georges Bank and Low at the mouth of Chesapeake Bay (@fig-exp-longfin). These patterns were driven by high exposure in sea surface temperatures, salinities, pH, and zooplankton biomass (@fig-fact-exp-longfin).

Longfin squid also received a High Exposure score in the previous assessment [@hare2016vulnerability]. This was driven by high temperature and ocean acidification scores [@hare2016vulnerability].

Mean Vulnerability for Longfin squid was **Low** (3.02 +/- 0.54) (@fig-sum-tab-longfin). Vulnerability remained Low on average when Exposure was calculated only with factors that were important to its distribution (@fig-sum-tab-longfin). Vulnerability was Moderate along the west coast of the Gulf of Maine and over Georges Bank, but Low throughout the rest of the species’ range (@fig-vuln-longfin).

Longfin squid also received a Low Vulnerability score in the previous Assessment [@hare2016vulnerability].

## Data Quality Metrics

### Life History Data Quality:

93% of data quality scores were greater than or equal to 2, indicating excellent data quality. No data gaps (mean attribute data quality score \< 2) were identified (@fig-sum-tab-longfin).

### Model Confidence Score:

Mean model confidence for longfin squid was 2.2 (+/- 0.27), indicating moderate confidence in the ensemble model. Experts stated that the model captured species distributions well and environmental drivers met expectations. The model AUC score was 0.83 indicating good performance.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
*Note: For an animated version of this plot, please see the online version of this document.*
:::

Longfin squid habitat grew significantly between 1993 and 2023. While core habitat was lost along the continental shelf, habitat area grew along the coastline (@fig-shifts-longfin). During this time, the weighted centroid shifted 9 km northeast. 

Under near future climate conditions, habitat area is predicted to continue expanding significantly. More core habitat loss is predicted along the continental shelf but more habitat is predicted to become available on the shelf itself and in nearshore areas (@fig-shifts-longfin). The weighted centroid is predicted to shift a further 18 km north. 

In the previous assessment, longfin squid received a High Distributional Vulnerability Rank score due to their mobility, migrations, and habitat preferences [@hare2016vulnerability].

| 2019-2023 | 9.3 km NE | 78,669 (+3,423) | 223,390 (+5,637) | 8.10 (+0.25) | 9.22 (+0.16) |
| 2031-2035 | 18.2 km N | 79,011 (+342) | 229,407 (+6,017) | 8.10 (0) | 9.22 (0) |

### Directional Effect:

Experts predicted that climate change would have **neutral** impacts on long-finned squid. Certainty was 95%. The short life-span of long-finned squid can make it challenging to understand the effects of climate change. In warmer temperatures, squid may grow faster and mature earlier, but they may also be negatively impacted by ocean acidification [@pecl2008potential] [@arkhipkin2015world]. In the previous assessment along the Northeast shelf, experts predicted that climate change would have a positive impact on long-finned squid, with a low amount of certainty [@hare2016vulnerability].

## Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution

Cephalopods have been shown to be sensitive to environmental variability and climate change, due to their short lifespan [@moustahfid2021ecological]. Inshore squids, such as longfin, may have complex responses to climate change. As temperatures increase, squids will likely hatch smaller and earlier, grow faster, mature at a smaller size, and have shorter life spans. They may also require more food and oxygen, but a reduced capacity to cope without food [@pecl2008potential]. Longfin squid recruitment may negatively be affected by impacts of increasing ocean acidification on the paralarval stage [@arkhipkin2015world]. Longfin squid raised under elevated pCO^2^ increased hatching time (\~24 hours longer) and had shorter mantle lengths as well as significantly reduced statolith surface area (by 25%) and abnormally shaped and porous statoliths [@kaplan2013adverse]. Abundance and distribution changes have been linked to the North Atlantic Oscillation, Gulf Stream, and surface fronts on the outer continental shelf [@dawe2007ocean] [@hendrickson2023cyclical] [@manderson2011ocean].

## Life History Synopsis

In the Northwest Atlantic, longfin squid are most abundant from Georges Bank to Cape Hatteras although their range expands from Newfoundland to the Gulf of Venezuela [@jacobson2005essential]. The North Atlantic stock undertakes seasonal migrations: moving offshore in the fall to overwinter along the shelf edge and slope and migrating inshore in the spring following warming water temperatures to spawn [@hatfield2002geographic]. More recent studies after the development of statolith aging techniques highlight a peak in spawning from late spring to summer [@hatfield2002geographic] [@macy2001seasonal] and hatching in late summer [@jacobson2005essential]. Some spawning occurs throughout the year both inshore and offshore depending on hatching month and length-at-age [@macy1994application] [@macy2001seasonal], with winter spawning thought to occur primarily south of Cape Hatteras [@hatfield2002geographic]. Eggs incubate for 11 - 27 days on sandy or muddy bottoms attached to solid substrate, with faster development times are warmer temperatures. The duration of the larval stage is unclear, but they occupy coastal surface waters. Once juveniles, they transition from inhabiting surface waters to a demersal lifestyle [@jacobson2005essential]. The Gulf Stream and warm core rings may facilitate the recruitment transport of larval and juvenile squid northward, but potential for inputs to the population from the Southeast U.S. Continental Shelf and offshore are difficult to quantify [@hatfield2002geographic]. Juveniles and adults are generally demersal and inhabit the continental shelf and upper slope to depths of 400 m. This varies seasonally, with adults occupying shallower habitats in summer and fall, and deeper habitats in the winter. Diel vertical migrations have been reported [@jacobson2005essential]. Juveniles consume planktonic organisms, primarily copepods. Their preferred prey type varies with size [@jacobson2005essential]. Larger individuals feed on crustaceans and small fish. Diets shift seasonally from crustacean-dominated in the spring to fish-dominated in the fall. Cannibalism is observed in individuals larger than 5 cm [@jacobson2005essential]. Longfin squid are prey for a variety of finfish, marine mammals, and birds [@jacobson2005essential]. Most statolith-aging studies suggest that longfin squid have a short lifespan of around 1 year or less, reaching maturity shortly before spawning and senescence [@macy2001seasonal]. Longfin squid are managed by the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council under the Mackerel, Squid, and Butterfish Fishery Management Plan. The stock is not overfished, and overfishing reference points are not available [@mafmc2025longfin].

Factors must explain at least 10% of variance in the ensemble model to be used to calculate total exposure."
```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| label: fig-radar-longfin
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
knitr::include_graphics(img_path)
```

Sea surface temperature, salinity, and small and large zooplankton biomass were important to the distribution of longfin squid (@fig-radar-longfin). Longfin are planktivores and prey size increases with body size [@jacobson2005essential]. Temperature plays an important role in development and major currents like the Gulf Stream play a large role in transport [@pecl2008potential], [@arkhipkin2015world] [@hatfield2002geographic]. When only these factors were used to calculate exposure, the mean score dropped to Moderate (1.7 +/- 0.87) (@fig-sum-imp-longfin). In this scenario, exposure was greatest along the middle of the continental shelf and Georges Bank, where high exposures overlapped for temperature, salinity, and zooplankton variables (@fig-exp-imp-longfin).

```{r}
  newest_index <- which.max(file_details$mtime)
  
  # Assign the newest file's path to img_path
  img_path <- found_files[newest_index]
} else {
  img_path <- NULL
}
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| lightbox: true
#| out-width: "100%"

#| fig-cap: "As in @fig-sum-tab-longfin for Longfin squid, but with only significant Exposure factors and the resulting Vulnerability Scores."
#| fig-pos: "H"

knitr::include_graphics(img_path)
```
